hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
Imagine following nearly 13 million real people for more than 10 years just to see what cholesterol level helps them live the longest. That is exactly what Korean scientists did in a giant 2019 study. They tracked 12.8 million adults who had check-ups between 2001 and 2004, and they kept watching until 2013. More than 694,000 people died during that long stretch.
The results were clear and surprising. Cholesterol and death formed a U-shape. Very low cholesterol was linked to higher death rates. So was very high cholesterol. The sweet spot for the longest life was 210 to 249 mg/dL for most adults. That is higher than many doctors call “ideal.” Younger people had a slightly lower best range, but still not the super-low numbers often pushed today.
Because the study lasted so many years, reverse causality is less likely to explain the low-cholesterol danger. Reverse causality means a hidden illness might lower your cholesterol right before it kills you. With more than a decade of follow-up, early sickness cannot easily account for the extra deaths seen in people who started with low cholesterol. The pattern held across ages and for both men and women.
The huge number of people—almost the entire adult population of a country—makes the findings hard to ignore. Smaller studies can be wrong by chance. This one is massive. It shows that moderately higher total cholesterol, not the lowest possible number, went with the best chance of living longer in this large group.
In short, the biggest study of its kind found that cholesterol levels in the low-to-mid 200s were tied to the longest lives, and the long tracking time makes it tougher to blame the higher death rates at low levels on reverse causality alone.
hits.draft_en:

Not medical advice, and it's one study. But it's worth asking your GP what your number actually means for you, not just chasing it as low as it'll go.

Doctors still slice into arthritic knees, scrape the cartilage, and flush out the joint hundreds of thousands of times a year—even though a major study proved the real surgery works no better than fake surgery.

In 2002, surgeon J. Bruce Moseley and his team published a carefully designed study in the New England Journal of Medicine. They took 180 patients with painful knee osteoarthritis who had already tried medicines and other treatments. The patients were randomly split into three groups. One group got the full arthroscopic surgery: the doctor washed out the knee with a lot of fluid, shaved rough cartilage, and trimmed any torn or worn pieces of the meniscus (the soft cushion in the knee). A second group got only the washing (lavage). The third group got a sham, or fake, surgery. Those patients were sedated, the surgeon made the same small skin cuts, and the operating room team made the sounds and motions of real surgery—but nothing ever went inside the joint.
Neither the patients nor the people checking their results knew who got the real surgery and who got the fake one. For two full years, researchers tracked pain and how well people could walk and climb stairs. At every check-up, the three groups looked the same. The real operations did not reduce pain or improve function any better than the pretend surgery. The confidence intervals even ruled out any meaningful difference. Patients in all groups felt a bit better, which the researchers attributed to the placebo effect—the power of believing you had a real treatment—plus the natural ups and downs of the condition.
At the time of the study, more than 650,000 of these arthroscopic procedures were already being done each year in the United States. Rates of pure “clean-out” surgeries for osteoarthritis later fell somewhat after guidelines advised against them, yet knee arthroscopy (especially for degenerative meniscus tears that often occur alongside arthritis) remains extremely common. Recent data still show hundreds of thousands of knee arthroscopies performed annually in the U.S. alone. The Moseley trial and later similar studies continue to show that, for typical age-related knee wear, the mechanical work inside the joint adds little or nothing beyond the placebo effect and standard non-surgical care.

Imagine a doctor in 1870s Naples locking his patients in a room and feeding them nothing but meat until their diabetes “disappeared.” That’s exactly what Italian physician Arnaldo Cantani did—and he claimed it worked for dozens of people.

Arnaldo Cantani (1837–1893) was a professor of medicine in Naples and an Italian senator. In an era before insulin existed, diabetes was often a death sentence. Sugar spilled into the urine, patients wasted away, and doctors had few tools. Cantani’s bold idea was simple but extreme: cut out every bit of carbohydrate and feed patients only animal foods.
His “Cantani system” meant meat, animal fats, fish, eggs, and sometimes limited alcohol. No bread, no pasta, no fruit, no sugar, and usually no milk or butter (because of the lactose). He kept patients on this exclusive meat diet for two to nine months until their urine tested free of sugar. He sometimes used short fasts if needed and added lactic acid in water to help digestion. To make sure people followed the rules, he reportedly locked some patients in rooms under strict supervision.
Cantani kept detailed notes on more than 150 cases. He reported that about 73 of his own patients—and many treated by other doctors—lost their symptoms and their urine sugar. He called this a “cure.” After the sugar cleared, he slowly added back green vegetables, cheese, nuts, and limited fruit, while warning patients to avoid starches and sweets for life. Many of his patients had eaten mostly bread, pasta, and sweets before they got sick.
This was real clinical work, not a modern clinical trial. Diagnosis was based on symptoms and urine sugar tests; doctors didn’t yet separate type 1 from type 2 diabetes. Results depended on strict compliance, and long-term data on heart health or other risks simply didn’t exist. Still, Cantani’s meat-based approach became known across Europe and influenced other physicians. Modern carnivore and low-carb communities often point to his work as early evidence that removing carbohydrates can reverse diabetic symptoms.
In short, long before today’s diet debates, an Italian doctor used an all-meat plan to treat a deadly disease—and documented results that still spark discussion more than 150 years later.

Richard Horton, editor-in-chief of The Lancet, concluded that medical journals had “devolved into information-laundering operations for the pharmaceutical industry.” 
This statement comes from his March 2004 New York Review of Books essay “The Dawn of McScience.” He described how companies sponsor meetings, pay speakers, have communications firms turn the talks into articles (often with minimal or no peer review), and then pay publishers large sums to run them as journal supplements. The result, he argued, is marketing dressed up as science that seeds the literature with weaker evidence used to promote products. 
Around the same period, in written and oral evidence to the UK House of Commons Health Select Committee (2004–2005), Horton described the journal–industry relationship as “somewhere between symbiotic and parasitic,” noting that it had swung too far toward the parasitic side. He highlighted financial pressures (e.g., companies promising large reprint orders if a favorable paper is published, or threatening to pull papers if criticism is not softened) and listed roughly 10 distorting practices, including: 
•  Manipulation or selective reporting of findings
•  Bias toward positive results in industry-sponsored studies
•  Hiding negative or adverse data
•  Ghostwriting
•  Lightly peer-reviewed supplements used for marketing
•  Undisclosed conflicts of interest
He stated that commercial sponsorship of research and its intrusion into academia represented “one of the gravest threats to the independent evaluation of new medicines—indeed to the notion of an independent science base,” and that the for-profit motive of the sector clashes with public-health values and independent scientific research. 
In a 2013 Lancet piece (“Falling out with pharma”), Horton withdrew the journal’s support from industry-linked guidance on doctor–pharma collaboration, saying the document’s claims did not match the evidence on company behavior regarding transparency, medical education, and prescribing influence. 
His better-known 2015 editorial (“Offline: What is medicine’s 5 sigma?”) was broader—arguing that “much of the scientific literature, perhaps half, may simply be untrue” due to small samples, invalid analyses, tiny effects, and “flagrant conflicts of interest”—but conflicts of interest (often industry-related) were explicitly part of that critique. 
These statements reflect Horton’s long-standing concerns about industry influence on the medical evidence base rather than a single one-off finding.

Many people choose a plant-based diet to cause less harm to animals and the planet, and that's an admirable goal. But good intentions don't guarantee good outcomes.

Grain and legume crops come with their own deaths. Harvesters, plows, and rodent poisons kill huge numbers of mice, birds, and other small animals every season, and those deaths are rarely counted. One estimate put it at about 55 animal deaths per 100 kg of usable protein from wheat, compared with about 2 from grass-fed beef.

The evidence is clear that no food system is free of death. The fair way to compare diets is by their full outcomes, not by which deaths are easiest to see.

If you're going to take or recommend testosterone therapy of any kind, you should watch this.

Hematocrit is the percentage of your blood that is red blood cells, essentially how thick and viscous your blood is. It costs a couple of dollars and it's on basically every blood panel ever run.

When you go on testosterone, your red blood cell count will very likely increase and, consequently, your hematocrit. That sounds great, and it's part of why you feel physically different and might experience an increase in energy. But it can get out of control fast.

Once you start getting north of 52 to 54 percent on hematocrit, you increase your risk of developing heart disease or suffering a serious cardiovascular event.

This is the cost of doing business with testosterone therapy. Pay attention to it.

According to the EPIC-Oxford study, the top two major causes of death among vegans are cancer and heart disease.
The European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition–Oxford (EPIC-Oxford) is one of the largest long-term cohort studies examining diet and health in the UK. 

A key 2016 analysis (Appleby et al., American Journal of Clinical Nutrition) pooled data from EPIC-Oxford and the Oxford Vegetarian Study, tracking more than 60,000 participants—including roughly 2,228 vegans—over more than a million person-years of follow-up. 

There were 5,294 deaths before age 90.
Among the 166 deaths recorded in the vegan group, cancer (malignant neoplasms) and circulatory/heart disease were the leading causes by absolute numbers. This mirrors patterns seen across the other diet groups and in the broader UK population. When researchers compared vegans directly with regular meat-eaters, there were no statistically significant differences in mortality from malignant cancer, circulatory disease, ischemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, or respiratory disease. 

Hazard ratios for these outcomes generally ranged from about 0.8 to 1.5, but confidence intervals were wide because of the relatively small number of vegan deaths.
All-cause mortality was also similar across diet groups. Vegans had a hazard ratio of 1.14 (95% CI 0.97–1.35) compared with regular meat-eaters—not a significant difference.
hits.draft_en:
Dr Shawn Baker cites the EPIC-Oxford study: among vegans in that UK cohort, the top two causes of death by raw count were cancer and heart disease — same as the wider population.

The careful bit: when researchers compared vegans with regular meat-eaters, there were no statistically significant differences in death rates from cancer, heart disease or several other causes. All-cause mortality was similar too.

So the headline "vegans die of cancer and heart disease" is true as a count, and also true of everyone else. The study doesn't prove vegan diets are safer or more dangerous on those endpoints. Don't let a chart cherry-pick your lunch.

What if the doctors teaching you, the researchers testing new drugs, and the journals you trust were all being paid by the same companies that sell those drugs?
Arnold Relman, who edited the New England Journal of Medicine for 14 years, believed that is exactly what was happening. In 1980 he warned about a new “medical-industrial complex”—a growing web of for-profit hospitals, labs, and companies that treat health care like a business instead of a service for sick people. Over time he became especially worried about the pharmaceutical industry’s influence. 
Relman said the drug companies were buying the medical profession. They paid for research, sponsored medical education classes, and funded the experts who wrote articles and guidelines. Academic medical centers and universities, he argued, were letting themselves become “paid agents” of the industry. In his view, this was disgraceful because doctors and scientists are supposed to put patients first, not company profits. 
He saw the problem in continuing medical education, where drug companies helped pay for the courses doctors must take to keep their licenses. He argued that education should be free of marketing pressure so doctors learn what is best for patients, not what sells the most pills. As editor, he made the New England Journal one of the first to require authors to disclose any money they received from companies whose products they wrote about. 
Relman thought the solution was bigger than better rules. He believed medicine should be non-profit, with doctors paid a salary instead of fees for every test or procedure, and with a simpler payment system that does not reward unnecessary care. He kept sounding the alarm for decades, saying the commercial side of medicine had grown even worse than he first predicted.

What if the “heart-healthy” low-fat, low-cholesterol diet that doctors have pushed for decades doesn’t just lower your LDL—it also makes you more likely to snap, slap, bite, or lash out?
That’s exactly what a series of controlled experiments on cynomolgus macaques (Macaca fascicularis) demonstrated in the 1990s. Jay R. Kaplan and colleagues housed groups of these highly social monkeys and fed them either high-fat, high-cholesterol diets or the kind of lower-fat, lower-cholesterol “prudent” diets recommended by the American Heart Association. Across multiple studies, the animals on the low-cholesterol regimens consistently showed more contact aggression—slapping, grabbing, grappling, and biting—along with more submissive displays and less affiliative behavior such as sitting in passive body contact or staying close to one another.
In one key experiment, juvenile monkeys eating a low-cholesterol diet were more aggressive and less social than their high-cholesterol counterparts; they also had lower levels of the serotonin metabolite 5-HIAA in their cerebrospinal fluid. Another within-subjects design switched animals from a very high-fat diet to a low-fat one and observed the same pattern: aggression rose while affiliation and proximity fell. Body weight stayed comparable, isolating the effect to the dietary cholesterol and fat change itself.
The proposed mechanism runs through serotonin. Low central serotonergic activity is one of the most reliable biological correlates of impulsivity and aggression across species. Cholesterol is a major component of neuronal membranes; reducing it appears to impair serotonin receptor function or signaling in brain regions that normally dampen impulsive and violent behavior. The result is a weaker “brake” on aggression.
These primate findings line up with human observations linking naturally low or medically lowered cholesterol to higher rates of suicide, accidents, and violence-related deaths. While the monkey data are experimental and the human data largely correlational, together they suggest that pushing cholesterol very low may carry behavioral costs for at least some individuals—costs that rarely make it into the standard public-health script about diet and heart disease.
hits.draft_en:
Dr Shawn Baker digs up 1990s monkey studies: macaques on low-fat, low-cholesterol "heart-healthy" diets got more aggressive — more slapping, grabbing and biting — and less social than monkeys on higher-fat, higher-cholesterol feed.

The researchers tied it to serotonin signalling in the brain. Cholesterol is part of nerve-cell membranes; pushing it very low may weaken the brake on impulsivity. Human data (more correlational) have linked very low cholesterol with higher rates of suicide, accidents and violence-related deaths.

Monkey trials aren't a prescription for your plate. But they are a reminder that "lower forever" on cholesterol isn't a free lunch, and behaviour sits in the same body as the heart.

What if the medical journals you trust most are really just fancy ads for drug companies? That is the blunt warning from Richard Smith, who ran the famous BMJ journal for 13 years.
In a 2005 essay, Smith said medical journals have become “an extension of the marketing arm of pharmaceutical companies.” He spent decades inside the system. He watched how the money worked. Drug ads bring in cash, but that is not the biggest problem. The real power comes from industry-funded studies. Companies pay for most of the big drug trials published in top journals. Between two-thirds and three-quarters of those trials come from drug makers. And those trials almost never show bad results for the company’s product. Smith pointed to dozens of studies proving that who pays for the research often shapes the answer.
A positive trial is worth far more than regular advertising. Companies buy thousands of reprints and hand them out to doctors. One big order can bring a journal more than a million dollars in pure profit. Editors know this. Many journals need that money to survive. So they keep publishing the industry studies. Readers treat those papers as pure science. They do not always see the marketing side.
Smith said it took him almost 25 years as an editor to fully wake up to the problem. He quoted the Lancet editor, who called journals “information laundering operations for the pharmaceutical industry.” Smith suggested a radical fix: stop publishing industry trials in journals. Put the raw results on public websites instead. Let journals focus on explaining and criticizing the science, not selling it.
His words still hit hard today. When the people who once ran the biggest journals say the system is broken, it is worth paying attention.

Doctors often give cortisone (steroid) shots straight into painful joints to calm swelling and ease pain. They work well for a short time. But growing research shows these shots may make arthritis worse over the long run, especially when used again and again.
In a careful 2017 study, people with knee arthritis got either a real cortisone shot or a saltwater shot every three months for two years. The cortisone group lost more cartilage—the smooth cushion that protects the bones—than the group that got the fake shot. Pain levels ended up about the same. The researchers said the repeated shots did not help and may have hurt the joint.
A newer 2025 study looked at MRI scans from hundreds of people in a big arthritis project. Those who got one cortisone shot showed more joint damage two years later than people who got no shot or who got a different gel-like injection (hyaluronic acid). The cortisone group had more cartilage breakdown. The other injection seemed to slow the damage.
A review of several studies found that people who received cortisone shots were about twice as likely to show signs of cartilage loss on scans. Some reports also describe rare but serious cases, especially in hips, where a joint collapses faster than expected after a shot.
Not every study agrees. Some long-term checks of real patients found no clear rise in knee replacements after cortisone shots. Still, the pattern is clear enough that many experts now urge caution.
Cortisone calms inflammation fast, but it can also slow the joint’s ability to repair itself. One or two shots for a bad flare may be fine. Frequent shots, though, look riskier for the structure of the joint.
Talk with your doctor about how often to use them, and ask about other options that ease pain without speeding up wear and tear. Your joints have to last a lifetime—treat them carefully.

What if the secret to living past 100 wasn’t just eating more vegetables—but keeping meat on your plate, especially when you’re already old and thin?
A big study from China followed more than 5,000 people who were already 80 or older. Researchers watched them for about 20 years to see who made it to 100. Most of the people who became centenarians ate meat. Those who avoided meat completely did worse. 
The people who followed a vegan diet—no meat, fish, eggs, or dairy—had the lowest chance of reaching 100. Compared with meat eaters, vegans were about 29% less likely to hit that age. Overall, anyone who stayed vegetarian was less likely to become a centenarian than people who ate meat. 
The difference showed up mainly among people who were underweight. Thin older adults who ate meat every day were much more likely to live to 100 than thin vegetarians. People who were a healthy weight didn’t show the same big gap. Those who still ate fish, eggs, or dairy did better than strict vegans.
Scientists think this happens because very old bodies need enough calories and protein to stay strong. Being underweight at that age raises the risk of frailty and early death. Meat helps supply those nutrients. The study doesn’t prove meat causes longer life, and it only looked at people already in their 80s in China. Still, the numbers were clear: the strictest plant-only diets were linked to the fewest people making it to 100.
hits.draft_en:

Most of the centenarians ate meat. Vegans had the lowest chance of reaching 100 — about 29% less likely than meat eaters. The gap showed up mainly in people who were underweight: thin older adults who ate meat every day did much better than thin vegetarians.

Imagine a baby orangutan still nursing from its mom at age seven or eight—clinging tight for years while learning to climb and forage. Now picture a human toddler already eating solid foods by age two. That huge difference in weaning time is one of the biggest puzzles in human evolution, and a 2012 study cracked it with a simple idea: eating meat.
Scientists looked at weaning times across 67 different mammals, from rodents to big cats to apes. They built a model that predicted when each species would stop nursing. The biggest factor was brain size—bigger brains take longer to develop, so animals with large brains tend to nurse longer. Body posture and movement also mattered a bit. But diet made a real difference too.
When the model left humans out and tried to predict our weaning time, it got it almost exactly right—about two years and four or five months after birth. That matched the average age from dozens of traditional human societies that don’t use modern formula or early solid foods. Chimpanzees and orangutans, our closest ape relatives, nurse for five to eight years. Humans stop much earlier.
The key difference? Carnivory—eating a significant amount of meat. The study concluded that adding meat to the diet was both necessary and sufficient to explain why humans wean so young. Meat is dense in calories and nutrients, so mothers can support a growing baby’s big brain without needing to nurse for years. Early weaning also lets mothers have babies more often, which helped human populations grow.
In short, the same rules that set weaning times across mammals also apply to us. Our early shift to eating meat didn’t just change what we put on our plates—it reshaped how long our kids stay dependent on milk and helped make human life history unique.

What if the real secret to “living” past 100 wasn’t healthy food or daily walks, but bad paperwork and collecting a pension after you’re already dead?
Scientist Saul Newman looked at the famous “blue zones”—places like Okinawa in Japan, Sardinia in Italy, and Ikaria in Greece—where people are said to live extra-long, healthy lives. He found a different story. The areas with the most reported 100- and 110-year-olds were usually the poorest, had the worst records of births and deaths, and often had shorter average lifespans than the rest of their country. 
In Japan, a government check found that about 82% of people listed as over 100 were actually missing or already dead. Families had sometimes kept collecting the pension for years. In Greece, a huge number of listed centenarians turned out to be dead or nonexistent while still getting payments. When the U.S. started requiring birth certificates, the number of people claiming to be over 110 dropped sharply. Many “validated” super-old people never had a real birth certificate at all. 
Newman also checked the lifestyle stories. Government surveys showed that people in Okinawa actually ate fewer vegetables than other Japanese and were not the healthiest group in the country. The blue zones ranked poorly for real old-age survival once the bad data was cleaned up. 
His research (still a preprint, not yet fully published in a journal) won an Ig Nobel Prize for making people laugh and then think. Supporters of blue zones say the ages were carefully checked with old church and government records. Newman says even consistent records can be wrong if the original age was faked. The debate continues, but his work shows that extreme age claims often depend more on messy paperwork and money than on special diets or secrets of long life.

Newman found the places with the most reported 100- and 110-year-olds were often the poorest with the worst birth and death records. In Japan a government check found about 82% of people listed as over 100 were missing or already dead, with families sometimes still collecting the pension.

hits.text:
Imagine Ice Age hunters so tall they looked down on almost everyone else—men averaging nearly six feet tall while tracking and killing woolly mammoths in frozen Europe 30,000 years ago. These were the Gravettians, tough people who thrived in one of the coldest times in human history.
They lived across Europe from about 33,000 to 21,000 years ago. Life was hard, but they were skilled and mobile. They followed animal herds across icy grasslands and built homes, sometimes using mammoth bones. They made sharp stone tools, nets, and beautiful art like the famous Venus figurines of women.
Their diet was mostly meat and fat. Mammoths were a favorite in places like the Czech Republic—scientists can see this in the chemicals left in their bones. They also hunted reindeer, horses, and wolves. Smaller animals like hares and foxes were caught with nets. Near the sea, they ate fish and seals. This rich food gave them huge amounts of protein and calories, perfect for staying strong in the cold. They crushed bones to get the fatty marrow inside.
That diet helped them grow tall and strong. Gravettian men usually stood between 5 feet 10 inches and 6 feet 2 inches, with an average around 6 feet. They were lean and muscular from constant hunting and walking. Women averaged about 5 feet 2 inches but were sturdy. Their high cheekbones and athletic builds made them stand out. Later, when people started farming and eating more grains, average height dropped.
The Gravettians show how a meat-heavy diet and active life in a harsh world could build some of the tallest ancient people we know. Their tools, art, and bones still tell the story of a powerful Ice Age culture.

My interest in fatty liver in lean people grew when I was invited to Asia to help study it. It's a pressing problem there. Many people look metabolically healthy on the scale, but their livers tell a different story.

It isn't unique to Asia. About 1 in 5 people with fatty liver are lean, and about 4 in 10 aren't obese. When the fat tissue under the skin can't expand well, extra fat gets pushed into the liver, even at a normal weight, and it can still lead to inflammation and scarring.

A normal BMI doesn't guarantee a healthy liver. Triglycerides and liver enzymes on routine bloodwork tell a person far more.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
Drug companies are quietly paying doctors and influencers to talk up their medicines online — and most people never see the full picture.
A 2024 study looked at doctors who posted about specific drugs or devices on X. Nearly all of them (93%) had taken money from the company that makes the product. Those payments added up to hundreds of thousands of dollars. The average doctor in the group received about $27,000 from the manufacturer. Most of the money came for speaking or consulting. Many of the posts were paid promotions, and some doctors never clearly said they were paid.
The numbers are even bigger for popular weight-loss drugs. One investigation found that two major companies paid more than 250,000 doctors and other prescribers over several years. The total spending topped $270 million. Some individual doctors received close to a million dollars. Companies say these payments help share science. Critics say the money can shape what doctors tell patients.
It is not only doctors. Celebrities and lifestyle influencers also get paid. In past cases the FDA sent warning letters after stars promoted drugs without mentioning risks. One famous example involved a well-known influencer and a morning-sickness pill. Similar problems have appeared with other paid posts.
A 2025 study of hundreds of popular social-media posts about common drugs found that 80% looked like unpaid promotions but carried signs of marketing. Only a tiny fraction used clear tags such as “#ad.” Drug companies themselves posted very few of them. Many posts talked about benefits but skipped serious side effects.
Patients see this content and ask their doctors about the drugs. In one survey, most doctors said patients had requested a medicine they first saw online, and many then wrote the prescription. Rules require companies to show both benefits and risks and to disclose payments, but enforcement has not kept up with the volume of posts.
The result is a system where money flows to the people patients trust most, yet the full story of those payments and the risks is often missing.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
What if the same advice doctors give to protect your heart—eat less fat and lower your cholesterol—might quietly raise the risk of violence behind bars?
A surprising body of research has found that people with lower cholesterol levels are more likely to act aggressively or commit violent crimes. In one large Swedish study of nearly 80,000 adults, those with cholesterol below the median were roughly twice as likely to later be arrested for violent offenses, even after accounting for age, education, and alcohol use. Similar patterns appear in other groups: Indian men with violent criminal records had lower total and LDL cholesterol than non-offenders, and forensic psychiatric patients with lower cholesterol spent more time in seclusion for violent incidents.
Scientists think the link may involve brain chemistry. Cholesterol helps cell membranes work properly. When levels drop, serotonin signaling can weaken. Lower serotonin is a well-known factor in impulsivity and aggression. Experiments with monkeys support this idea—those put on low-fat, low-cholesterol diets became more aggressive and less social than monkeys on higher-fat diets.
Prison studies add another layer. In a landmark UK trial with young adult inmates, giving daily vitamin, mineral, and essential fatty acid supplements cut disciplinary offenses by about 26% overall and serious violent incidents by 37%, compared with placebo. Similar nutrient trials in other prisons have produced average drops in violence around 30%. Prison diets are often low in quality fats and key nutrients, which may compound the problem.
These findings do not prove that low cholesterol directly causes violence, and high cholesterol still raises heart-disease risk. They do suggest that aggressively lowering cholesterol—or feeding nutrient-poor diets—could have behavioral side effects worth considering, especially in populations already at higher risk for aggression. The evidence points to a possible trade-off: what’s good for arteries may not always be good for impulse control.

Fiber is helpful, but helpful isn't the same as essential.

The glucose benefit comes from soluble fiber, which slows how quickly starches and sugar from a meal reaches the blood. Insoluble fiber does little for blood sugar.

So soluble fiber's value for glucose control depends on how much glucose there is to slow down. With carb-heavy meals, it can make a meaningful difference. With low-carb meals, there's less to blunt, and the value mostly depends on whether a person may still want some fiber to keep bowel movements regular.

What if the man who ordered some of the most brutal murders in American history also told his followers that killing animals was wrong? Charles Manson, the cult leader behind the 1969 Tate-LaBianca killings, built a twisted world where human lives meant little—but animals were supposedly off-limits.

Manson and his “Family” lived on Spahn Ranch in California. Followers later said he banned meat because eating it meant killing an animal. One ranch hand remembered the rule clearly: you could not eat meat “because you were killing an animal. It was crazy.” In a 1970 courtroom rant, Manson attacked meat-eaters, saying they killed “things that are better than you are” while calling his own people killers. He painted himself as someone who understood the value of life—yet he sent followers to slaughter pregnant actress Sharon Tate and others in gruesome attacks.

There is no clear proof Manson followed a strict vegan or low-fat diet every day, especially later in prison. What is clear is the sharp contrast: he and his group talked about protecting animals while planning and carrying out human murders. Drugs, control, and Manson’s own personality drove the violence far more than any meal plan.
Some researchers have studied whether low cholesterol (often linked to very low-fat diets) connects with higher aggression. Large studies of thousands of people have found that men with lower cholesterol levels were more likely to commit violent crimes later. Experiments with monkeys showed that animals switched to low-fat, low-cholesterol food became more aggressive and spent less time in friendly contact. Scientists think low cholesterol might affect brain chemicals like serotonin that help control impulses. 

These links are real in the data, but they do not prove that a low-fat diet turns someone into a killer. Most people who eat less fat never become violent, and Manson’s crimes had many other causes.
The Manson story shows how words about “kindness” can hide something darker. A man who claimed animals should not be harmed led a group that treated people as disposable. Diet may play a small role in mood and behavior for some, but it does not explain or excuse the calculated evil that happened under his orders.

What if the people who spent their whole lives paying taxes suddenly got told their favorite food was bad for the planet? In Copenhagen, Denmark, that is roughly what happened to some of the oldest and most fragile residents in city nursing homes.

City leaders created a food plan to cut climate pollution from meals by about 25 percent. The plan includes written advice for nursing homes. It says residents should get no more than 500 grams of cooked meat each week. Of that, only 80 grams should be beef, veal, or lamb. That is less than one small hamburger. 

The advice also suggests meat on hot meals only five days a week, and beef no more than once a week. Officials called these ideas “recommended amounts,” not strict rules.
Even so, the advice changed real meals. Some kitchens began serving two or three vegetarian meals a week. Reports from the city’s elderly council said a few residents could only get a hamburger on their birthday. Staff sometimes turned down requests for beef because it would hurt the home’s climate numbers. In a few cases people were steered toward apples instead of bananas because bananas have a higher climate cost. One analysis even found kitchen workers saying birthday wishes for beef were refused for CO2 reasons.

Imagine a drug for a terrible disease like Alzheimer’s gets the government’s green light—even though a team of outside experts said “no way,” the company’s own big study failed, and the price tag was $56,000 a year. That is exactly what happened with Aduhelm in 2021, and many people say it shows how drug companies can push the FDA too hard.

Aduhelm is a medicine made by Biogen to treat Alzheimer’s disease. It is supposed to clear sticky clumps called amyloid plaques from the brain. Biogen ran two big studies. One looked promising for some patients. The other failed. The FDA’s own math experts said the results were confusing and did not prove the drug helped people think better or remember more. An outside panel of doctors and scientists voted almost unanimously against approving it.

Still, the FDA approved Aduhelm in June 2021 under a special “accelerated” path. This path lets a drug reach patients faster if it affects a lab marker (like plaque) that might later lead to real benefits. The agency switched to this faster path late in the process. Internal documents and a later congressional report showed that FDA staff and Biogen held more than 100 meetings, calls, and emails. They worked unusually closely together, even helping shape briefing materials. Several high-level FDA leaders pushed the approval while other scientists inside the agency strongly disagreed. Three members of the outside expert panel resigned in protest.

Critics call this a clear case of corporate capture—when a company has too much influence over the people who are supposed to regulate it. The FDA gets a large share of its drug-review money from fees paid by the same companies it oversees. Officials often leave the agency for high-paying jobs in the drug industry. In Aduhelm’s case, the close teamwork, ignored expert advice, and weak proof of real patient benefit raised serious questions about whether industry pressure outweighed solid science. Biogen later stopped selling the drug in 2024 after weak sales and ongoing doubts. The episode remains one of the strongest recent examples of conflict-of-interest worries at the FDA.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Vitamin C and glucose compete for entry into cells, and glucose often wins.

In tissue from the human small intestine, glucose cut vitamin C uptake by more than half. Other gut transporters that carry the oxidized form of vitamin C are blocked by glucose at very low concentrations. In both humans and mice, higher blood glucose went with less vitamin C inside red blood cells, and those cells were more fragile.

This helps explain why people with chronically high blood sugar can run low on vitamin C even when they're well fed, and why scurvy still turns up in patients with obesity and diabetes. The evidence is clear that a person's vitamin C status depends on more than intake. The amount of glucose competing with it matters too.
